reasons.title: What to verify before adopting
reasons.subtitle: For a real adoption, ask the organization about health history, compatibility, responsible contacts, and support.

cards.title: Health history
cards.text: Ask the organization which health and vaccination records exist, what is known about neutering, and which care needs should be assessed with a veterinarian.

checklist.title: New home checklist
checklist.subtitle: Details that make adaptation easier.
items: Sturdy screens on open windows; suitable protection for accessible balconies.
Litter box in an accessible, quiet spot.
Food and water in separate, accessible locations.
A safe place to retreat and rest.
Scratching surfaces and opportunities for play.
Feeding planned around the cat's needs, with veterinary guidance.
Vaccination: ask the organization for records and consult a veterinarian.
Interaction and play that respect the cat's preferences.
checklist.sourceWindows: Open windows and balconies: ASPCA — High-Rise Syndrome: Lifesaving Tips for Cat Parents (2023).
checklist.sourceEnvironment: Litter box, resources, rest, play, and interaction: FelineVMA — Your Cat’s Environmental Needs (2026, PDF).
checklist.sourceFeeding: Feeding plan: FelineVMA — Feline Feeding Programs (caregiver guidance).
checklist.sourceVaccination: Source on vaccination: WSAVA — 2024 Guidelines for the Vaccination of Dogs and Cats (PDF in Portuguese, for veterinarians).
checklist.sourceNote: The ASPCA recommends sturdy screens on open windows and warns about falls from balconies; protection should be assessed for each home. The guidance on environment, feeding, and interaction is general and does not replace an individual veterinary assessment.

items.text: In an apartment, check window safety and provide separate, accessible places for water, food, the litter box, and rest.
A cat that seems wary may seek shelter. Offer a safe place and let the cat choose when to approach.
When bringing a new cat into a home with resident cats, plan a gradual introduction, watch their reactions, and keep separate spaces available.

faq.title: Questions for a real adoption
faq.subtitle: Use these answers as a starting point and confirm everything with the responsible organization.

items.q: Do I need experience with cats?
items.a: Not necessarily. Check whether the organization offers guidance and whether you can meet the animal’s needs.

items.q: Can I adopt if I rent?
items.a: Confirm the property rules and ask the organization which safety measures and features of the space to consider for this cat.

items.q: How long does a real adoption take?
items.a: Timing varies by organization, screening, and animal. This project does not conduct or estimate real adoption processes.

items.q: How can I learn about the cat's health history?
items.a: Ask the organization for health records and what is known about vaccination, neutering, deworming, and ongoing care. Discuss this cat's needs with a veterinarian.
items.sourceVaccination: Source on vaccination: WSAVA — 2024 Guidelines for the Vaccination of Dogs and Cats (PDF in Portuguese, for veterinarians).

hero.title: What responsible adoption involves
hero.subtitle: Assess your routine, costs, safety, and long-term commitments before contacting a real organization.

items.title: Your routine
items.text: Consider the available time, budget, and changes that daily care will require.

items.title: The cat's needs
items.text: Plan safe places, environmental resources, and veterinary care according to the cat's needs.
items.sourceEnvironment: Source on environmental needs: FelineVMA (PDF in English).

items.title: Responsible organization
items.text: Verify who is responsible for the cat, which information is documented, and how post-adoption support works.

list.title: Before adopting
items: Confirm that the home allows animals and can receive suitable safety protection.
Plan recurring expenses and a reserve for veterinary care.
Assess the time available for interaction, cleaning, and enrichment.
Consider children, other animals, and foreseeable changes to the routine.
Verify the organization's identity and the source of information about the cat.
Understand the adoption agreement and the support offered after adoption.

facts.title: What to ask about the cat
facts.subtitle: Ask the organization what is known about the real animal's history and needs.

items.title: Health and history
items.text: Ask the organization which health records exist, how the cat is fed, and what ongoing care it receives. Take clinical questions to a veterinarian.

items.title: Observed behavior
items.text: Ask which behaviors were observed and in which environments, without treating the profile as a guarantee.

items.title: Adaptation
items.text: Ask the organization how to prepare for the cat's arrival, plan for coexistence with animals already at home, and seek guidance suited to the species involved if difficulties arise.

hero.title: Prepare for a responsible adoption
hero.subtitle: Review questions, care needs, and steps to confirm with the organization responsible for the animal.

requirements.title: What to confirm with the organization
requirements.subtitle: Each organization defines its own criteria. Ask why each requirement exists and how your data will be used.
items: Which documents are requested and why.
Which safety conditions the home must meet.
Whether follow-up visits will occur and how they will be arranged.
Which vaccination records are available, and which care needs should be discussed with the veterinarian?
How does the organization recommend planning interaction and play for this cat?
Which commitments are included in the responsible adoption agreement.
requirements.sourceVaccination: Source on vaccination: WSAVA — 2024 Guidelines for the Vaccination of Dogs and Cats (PDF in Portuguese, for veterinarians).

support.title: Support after adoption
support.text: Ask who can provide guidance during adaptation, through which channels, and for how long.

tips.title: Settling into a new home
tips.subtitle: General guidance to prepare for a cat's arrival and respect their pace.

items.title: A quiet room to start
items.text: When a cat arrives in a new home, start with a quiet room that has food, water, and a litter box. Once the cat seems comfortable, gradually let them explore other rooms.

items.title: A safe place to retreat
items.text: FelineVMA recommends giving each cat a safe place to retreat or rest, with the ability to enter and exit from at least two sides if threatened. Examples include cardboard boxes, carriers, and elevated perches.

items.title: Let the cat set the pace
items.text: Respect each cat's individual preferences and let them initiate and control contact. Do not force interaction; some cats are less comfortable with petting or being held.

tips.sourceMoving: Source: ASPCA — Moving With Your Pet (webpage).
tips.sourceEnvironment: Source: Feline Veterinary Medical Association (FelineVMA), Your Cat’s Environmental Needs: Practical Tips for Cat Caregivers (2026; PDF).
tips.sourceNote: The ASPCA source addresses moving to a new home; it is used here as general guidance for a cat's arrival. These tips do not replace an individual veterinary assessment.

article.imageAlt: Cat playing on a scratching post
article.title: How to introduce a new cat to resident cats
article.author: Written by Lucas Alves
article.p1: Introduce the new cat to resident cats gradually. The process may take a few days to several months and, in some cases, longer. Move ahead only when every cat is comfortable with the current step.
article.h1: 1. Check health and prepare the space
article.p2: Before starting the introduction, make sure every cat has had a recent veterinary check-up and ask the veterinarian about testing the newcomer for common contagious diseases. If a resident cat is in poor health or is a senior with health concerns, seek veterinary advice before bringing in another cat. Provide each cat with a separate set of resources and one extra of each type. Keep resources accessible and visually separated. Prepare a transition room for the newcomer with its own food, water, litter box, scratching surface, hiding places, and elevated resting spots. Keep the cats separated when no one is supervising them.
article.p3: Once the newcomer explores the room confidently, swap blankets or soft toys between their spaces. After a few days, if every cat accepts these scents, use a soft cloth carrying one cat's scent to gently rub the others' cheeks and chin. Repeat until every cat tolerates this scent transfer. Signs such as hissing, growling, avoiding the item, acting differently, or eliminating outside the litter box may indicate tension; wait before moving ahead.
article.h3: 3. Play on opposite sides of a closed door
article.p4: If every cat tolerates scent transfer, offer short play sessions without visual contact on opposite sides of a closed door. If a cat hisses or growls, stop, increase the distance between the cats, and do not discipline them. Once every cat is comfortable with the earlier steps, keep the resident cats in another room with the door closed while the newcomer briefly explores shared areas. Then return the newcomer to the transition room and let the resident cats choose when to return to those areas.
article.h4: 4. Move from visual contact to supervised meetings
article.p5: When every cat is comfortable with the earlier steps, allow short visual sessions through a secure, transparent barrier. Watch their body language and vocalizations; if any cat seems uncomfortable, end the session and return to an earlier step. Only then arrange short, supervised physical-proximity sessions in a large room. Use a harness and leash only if the cats are already comfortable with them; use a partially covered carrier only if it is familiar and has been a positive experience. If tension appears, stop the interaction and block visual contact with a barrier such as a towel or piece of cardboard. Do not pick up the cats during a tense moment. Create distance before returning to an earlier step. Use toys or treats to reward calm behavior and gradually increase the time together without forcing interaction.
article.source: Feline Veterinary Medical Association (FelineVMA). Step-by-Step Guide: How to Introduce a New Cat to Other Cats in Your Home (2026, PDF).
article.sourceNote: This educational summary does not replace an individual veterinary assessment.
